desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. The result is also returned as an array of values from head to tail.

Group the nodes by the parity of their position (not their value). Positions are counted from 1: the 1st, 3rd, 5th, ... nodes are the odd-position nodes and the 2nd, 4th, ... nodes are the even-position nodes. Rearrange the list so that all odd-position nodes come first, followed by all even-position nodes, and inside each group the original relative order is kept. Return the values of the new list.

For example [1,2,3,4,5] becomes [1,3,5,2,4] and [2,1,3,5,6,4,7] becomes [2,3,6,7,1,5,4]. Aim for O(1) extra space by relinking the existing nodes.
hints: Imagine two separate lists being built while you walk: one for odd positions and one for even positions.
Keep odd and even pointers, plus the head of the even list (evenHead = head.next) so you can find it again at the end.
In each round do odd.next = even.next; odd = odd.next and then even.next = odd.next; even = even.next, as long as even and even.next exist. Finally attach odd.next = evenHead.
editorial: Because every odd-position node is followed by an even-position node and vice versa, you can unzip the list in place. odd starts at the head and even at the second node; the first node of the even chain is saved in evenHead. Repeatedly let the odd pointer jump over the even node to the next odd node, then let the even pointer jump over that odd node to the next even node.

When the loop ends, odd is the last odd-position node; link it to evenHead. The even chain already ends with null. The work is one pass, O(n) time and O(1) space. Remember it is the position that matters; sorting by value parity is a different problem.
